title: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
summary: How allocators carve big regions into small blocks: bump arenas that free everything at once, buddy blocks that merge with one XOR, and slab caches of ready-made objects, plus how Linux stacks them.
outcomes: Explain internal vs external fragmentation and which freedom each of bump, buddy and slab gives up
Compute bump-allocator addresses and padding for a sequence of aligned requests
Trace buddy splits and merges, finding a buddy with p XOR 2^k and the merged start with AND
Compute objects per slab, leftover bytes and slab colors, and explain why object caching saves time
Choose an allocator for a workload and reason about kmalloc size-class waste

lessons.title: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory

blocks.md:
From the mmap course you know how a process gets memory from the kernel: `mmap` (or `brk`) hands back a large, page-aligned region, at the cost of a system call and at least one whole page. A program that builds a million 24-byte list nodes cannot afford one system call and one 4 KiB page per node.

So every runtime puts an **allocator** in between: a library (or kernel subsystem) that grabs big regions rather rarely and **carves** them into the small blocks that code actually asks for.

The hardest version of the job is a general-purpose `malloc`: any size, in any order, freed in any order. The classic design keeps a **free list** of holes. To allocate, it searches the list for a hole that is big enough (for example the first one, *first fit*), **splits** off what it needs, and keeps the rest as a smaller hole. On free it tries to **coalesce** the block with free neighbors so holes grow back.

The figure uses a tiny 128-byte heap drawn as 8 slots of 16 bytes.

blocks.title: A 128-byte heap that has 32 free bytes but cannot give out 32

scenes.caption: An empty 128-byte heap. Simplified: real allocators also store a small header per block, which we ignore here.
Five requests arrive: A 32 B, B 16 B, C 32 B, D 16 B, E 32 B. Each is placed right after the previous one, and the heap is now full.
The program frees B and D. Their neighbors (A, C, E) are still in use, so there is nothing to coalesce with: we have two separate 16-byte holes.
Now a 32-byte request arrives. 32 bytes are free in total, but no single hole is 32 bytes long, so the request fails (or the allocator must ask the OS for more memory).

blocks.md:
Two kinds of waste show up in every allocator, and this course measures each design against both:

- **Internal fragmentation**: space wasted *inside* a block because the allocator handed out more than was asked for (rounding, alignment padding).
- **External fragmentation**: free memory that exists but is split into pieces too small to satisfy a request, as in the last scene.

On top of that, a general free list costs *time*: finding a fit can mean walking many list nodes scattered across memory, which Bonwick notes also causes cache and TLB misses.

blocks.prompt: Suppose instead the allocator only ever had to serve *one* size, say 16-byte objects. Could the failure in the last scene happen?
blocks.reveal: No. If every block is 16 bytes, every hole is exactly one usable block, so any free slot satisfies any request. External fragmentation of the kind shown here needs *different* sizes competing for the same space. That observation is the heart of the slab allocator in lesson 4.

blocks.md:
The three designs in this course each win by **refusing part of the general problem**:

1. **Bump / arena**: objects can only be freed all at once. Allocation becomes a pointer add.
2. **Buddy**: sizes are rounded up to powers of two and blocks are aligned to their size, so a block's neighbor can be found with one bit flip and merged cheaply.
3. **Slab**: each cache serves exactly one object size (often one type), so fitting is trivial and objects can even stay initialized between uses.

Real systems stack them: the Linux kernel runs a buddy allocator for pages with a slab allocator on top, and many programs add arenas for short-lived data.

Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

blocks.question: In the last scene, 32 bytes are free yet a 32-byte request fails. Which term names this problem?
options: Internal fragmentation, because the blocks are too large for their contents
External fragmentation, because the free space is split into holes smaller than the request
A memory leak, because B and D were never returned to the allocator
Alignment padding, because 32-byte blocks must start on a 32-byte boundary
blocks.explain: B and D were freed correctly, so it is not a leak. The free bytes exist but are scattered into two 16-byte holes, which is external fragmentation. Internal fragmentation is waste *inside* a handed-out block.

blocks.question: Why does a program not simply call `mmap` for every 24-byte object?
options: mmap cannot return memory smaller than a page, and each call is a system call, so it is both wasteful and slow
mmap memory cannot be written to until it is passed through malloc
mmap always returns memory on a different NUMA node
mmap regions are freed automatically after one function returns
blocks.explain: mmap works in whole pages (4 KiB on typical x86-64) and costs a kernel entry per call. An allocator amortizes both costs by carving many small objects out of one mapping.

lessons.title: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add

blocks.md:
The simplest allocator owns one **chunk** of memory and one **bump pointer** inside it. Everything before the pointer is allocated; everything after it is free. To allocate, check that the request still fits before the end of the chunk and move the pointer forward by the request size. That is the whole algorithm, as both the bumpalo documentation and Nick Fitzgerald's write-up put it.

The catch: there is no general way to free one object in the middle. Instead you free *everything at once* by moving the pointer back to the start. A chunk used this way is often called an **arena** or **region**.

One real-world detail the pseudo-code skips is **alignment** (from the pointers and alignment course: a `u64` must start at an address divisible by 8). Before bumping, the pointer is rounded up to the requested alignment with the usual power-of-two trick $(p + a - 1) \mathbin{\&} \lnot(a - 1)$. The bytes skipped by rounding are **padding**, the bump allocator's only internal fragmentation.

blocks.caption: Same logic as the upward-bumping Rust example in Fitzgerald's post, written in C. A real version also checks the additions for overflow.

blocks.md: Let us run it on a 64-byte chunk at address `0x1000` (so `end = 0x1040`) with six requests: `a` a 1-byte `u8`, `b` an 8-byte `u64` (align 8), `c` a 4-byte `u32` (align 4), `d` a 3-byte array of `u8`, `e` another `u64`, and `f` a 32-byte array of four `u64`. The figure draws the chunk as eight 8-byte words.

blocks.title: Six allocations bumped into one 64-byte chunk

scenes.caption: Fresh chunk: ptr = start = 0x1000. All 64 bytes are on the free side of the pointer.
a (1 byte, align 1) lands at 0x1000. ptr moves to 0x1001, in the middle of word 0.
b needs 8-byte alignment, so 0x1001 rounds up to 0x1008: 7 bytes of padding are skipped. b occupies 0x1008 to 0x100F and ptr becomes 0x1010.
c (4 bytes, align 4) fits at 0x1010 with no padding, then d (3 bytes, align 1) at 0x1014. ptr is now 0x1017.
e (u64) rounds 0x1017 up to 0x1018 (1 byte of padding) and ends at 0x1020. Total padding so far: 8 bytes out of 32 used.
f (32 bytes, align 8) starts exactly at 0x1020 and ends at 0x1040 = end. The chunk is full; the next request, even 1 byte, makes bump_alloc return NULL.
bump_reset sets ptr back to 0x1000. All six objects are freed in one store, no matter how many there were. Any pointer to them is now dangling.

blocks.title: Tracing bump_alloc on the same chunk

scenes.caption: Allocate b: size 8, align 8, with ptr = 0x1001 left over from a.
Round up: (0x1001 + 7) & ~7 = 0x1008. The 7 bytes in between are padding.
The new end of the allocation is 0x1008 + 8 = 0x1010, which is not past end (0x1040), so the request fits.
Commit the new pointer and return the aligned address. That is one add, one mask, one add, one compare, one store.
Later, with the chunk full (ptr = 0x1040), a 1-byte request computes new_ptr = 0x1041 > end and gets NULL.
bump_reset frees everything at once by restoring ptr to start.

blocks.prompt: Fitzgerald's post argues you should start the pointer at the **end** of the chunk and bump **downwards** (subtract the size, then round *down* to the alignment). Using the same six requests, where does `a` land and how much padding is used in total?
blocks.reveal: Bumping down, `a` lands at `0x103F` (the last byte). Then `b` computes 0x103F minus 8 = 0x1037, rounds down to 0x1030, wasting 7 bytes; `c` at 0x102C, `d` at 0x1029, `e` rounds 0x1021 down to 0x1020 (1 byte), and `f` fills 0x1000 to 0x101F. Same 8 bytes of padding, same 64 bytes used. The win is speed, not space: rounding down needs no addition, so it has no overflow check, and the compiled code has one fewer branch.

blocks.md:
**What happens when the chunk is full?** Production arenas do not fail. bumpalo allocates a new chunk from the global allocator and keeps bumping there; LLVM's `BumpPtrAllocator` does the same with backing slabs (4096 bytes by default in its template) and puts allocations above a size threshold into their own slab. Resetting or dropping the arena releases all chunks together.

**What about destructors?** Resetting the pointer does not run them. bumpalo's docs say this explicitly: objects' `Drop` implementations are not invoked unless you wrap them in its arena-aware `Box`.

scenes.caption: Handling one request (or compiling one function): many objects are created during the phase...
...and with malloc each one would need its own free, at its own time. Every free is bookkeeping and a chance for a leak or double free.
With an arena, every phase-local object simply lives until the phase ends, and one reset frees them all. Anything that must outlive the phase (the result) is copied out first.

blocks.md: "Arena" means different things in different allocators. In this lesson it is a bump region freed all at once. In jemalloc (and glibc malloc) an *arena* is an independent general-purpose heap with its own locks, used so threads contend less; you still free objects one by one there.

Bump allocation costs a few instructions and has no per-object free. It is ideal when a group of objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compiler pass) and wrong when objects die at unrelated times, because one long-lived object keeps the whole arena alive.

blocks.question: A server bump-allocates parsed headers into a per-request arena and resets it when the response is sent. A cache stores a pointer to one parsed header so later requests can reuse it. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because resetting the arena only moves a pointer and does not change the bytes
Memory leaks, because the header is never freed
The cached pointer dangles: after reset the next request bump-allocates over the same bytes
The arena must be locked, because a bump pointer cannot be reset while other pointers exist
blocks.explain: Reset makes the whole chunk free again, and the very next request reuses those addresses. The cached pointer now aliases unrelated data. Objects that outlive the phase must be copied out (or allocated elsewhere).

blocks.question: A bump pointer sits at offset 13 in a chunk. The next request is 16 bytes with alignment 8. At which offset does the object start, and where does the pointer end up (bumping upwards)?
options: Starts at 13, pointer ends at 29
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 32
Starts at 8, pointer ends at 24
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 29
blocks.explain: Round 13 up to a multiple of 8: (13 + 7) & ~7 = 16. Then add the size: 16 + 16 = 32. The 3 bytes at offsets 13 to 15 are padding.

lessons.title: The buddy allocator: split in halves, merge with one XOR

blocks.md:
The **binary buddy** system (devised by Knowlton in 1965 and described by Knuth) attacks the slowest part of a general allocator: coalescing. It makes two rules:

1. Every block is a power of two in size: $2^k$ units for some **order** $k$.
2. Every block of order $k$ starts at an offset that is a multiple of $2^k$.

The allocator keeps one free list per order. In the Linux page allocator the unit is a page, so an order-3 block is 8 contiguous pages.

**Allocate** order $k$: take a block from the order-$k$ list. If it is empty, take a block from the next higher non-empty order and **split** it in half repeatedly. Each split produces two **buddies**; one half continues down, the other goes on the free list one order lower.

**Free** a block of order $k$: if its buddy is also free and of the same order, remove the buddy from its list, **merge** the two into one block of order $k+1$, and repeat one level up. Stop when the buddy is in use or the top order is reached.

blocks.title: Splitting and merging in a 16-page buddy region

scenes.caption: A 16-page region managed as one free block of order 4 (2^4 = 16 pages). Cell numbers are page frame numbers (pfn). Free lists: order 4 holds pfn 0.

Allocate A, 1 page (order 0). No order-0 block exists, so the order-4 block is halved four times. Each split puts the unused half on a lower free list: order 3 at pfn 8, order 2 at 4, order 1 at 2, order 0 at 1.
Allocate B, 2 pages (order 1). The order-1 list already has pfn 2, so no split is needed: B gets pages 2 and 3.
Allocate C, 3 pages. Buddy blocks are powers of two, so 3 rounds up to 4 (order 2): C gets pfn 4 to 7 and page 7 is wasted inside the block. Free lists: order 0 at 1, order 3 at 8.
Free B (pfn 2, order 1). Its buddy is 2 XOR 2 = pfn 0, but pages 0 and 1 are not a free order-1 block (A holds page 0). No merge: pfn 2 goes on the order-1 list.

Free A (pfn 0, order 0). Buddy 0 XOR 1 = 1 is free at order 0: merge into an order-1 block at 0. Its buddy 0 XOR 2 = 2 is free at order 1: merge again into an order-2 block at pfn 0. The next buddy (pfn 4) is C, so we stop.
Free C (pfn 4, order 2). Buddy 4 XOR 4 = 0 is a free order-2 block: merge to order 3 at 0. Buddy 0 XOR 8 = 8 is a free order-3 block: merge to order 4. The region is whole again.

blocks.md: Why can the allocator find a buddy so cheaply? Because of rule 2. A block of order $k$ at offset $p$ has its low $k$ bits zero. Its buddy is the other half of the order-$(k+1)$ block that contains it, and the two halves differ only in bit $k$. So the buddy's offset is $p$ with bit $k$ flipped, and the merged block starts at whichever of the two is lower.

blocks.caption: Linux computes exactly this: __find_buddy_pfn returns page_pfn ^ (1 << order), and __free_one_page sets combined_pfn = buddy_pfn & pfn.
Excerpts from the kernel source. Before merging, Linux also checks that the buddy really is a free block of the same order (page_is_buddy).

blocks.md: In Linux, each memory zone has an array `free_area[NR_PAGE_ORDERS]`, one entry per order. `MAX_PAGE_ORDER` defaults to 10 (an architecture can override it), so there are 11 orders and the largest block is $2^{10} = 1024$ pages, which is 4 MiB with 4 KiB pages. Each order's list is further split by *migrate type* (movable, unmovable, and so on) to fight long-term fragmentation; per-CPU lists of small blocks sit in front. You can see the free counts per order in `/proc/buddyinfo`: each column is the number of free blocks of order 0, 1, 2, and so on, which tells you the largest contiguous allocation that can currently succeed.

blocks.prompt: A caller asks the buddy allocator for 65 pages. What block size does it get, and what fraction of that block is wasted?
blocks.reveal: 65 is just above 64, so it rounds up to the next power of two: 128 pages (order 7). The waste is (128 minus 65) / 128 = 49.2 percent. With binary buddy rounding, any request of $2^k + 1$ units wastes just under half its block. This is the internal fragmentation price paid for cheap merging.

blocks.title: Rounding waste: powers of two vs finer size classes

curves.label: waste with k classes per doubling

scenes.caption: k = 1 is binary buddy: every request rounds up to a power of two. Waste is zero at exact powers and jumps to almost 50 percent just above them.
k = 2 adds one class halfway (in this geometric model, about 1.41 times each power of two). Worst-case waste falls to about 29 percent.

k = 4 cuts worst-case waste to about 16 percent. Simplified model: real allocators pick integer class sizes, but the tradeoff is the same: more classes means less rounding waste but more free lists to keep stocked.

blocks.md: The buddy allocator does not eliminate external fragmentation. A single allocated page in the middle of an otherwise free region blocks every merge above it, so a system can have plenty of free pages and still fail an order-9 request. That is why Linux tracks migrate types and can compact memory.

Buddy trades internal fragmentation (power-of-two rounding, up to about 50 percent) for fast, simple coalescing: the buddy is one XOR away. It suits page-granular, physically contiguous memory, which is why Linux uses it for its page allocator and builds smaller allocators on top.

blocks.question: A free block of order 2 starts at pfn 12. Where is its buddy, and if the buddy is also free, where does the merged order-3 block start?
options: Buddy at pfn 16; merged block starts at 12
Buddy at pfn 14; merged block starts at 12
Buddy at pfn 8; merged block starts at 8
Buddy at pfn 4; merged block starts at 4
blocks.explain: 12 in binary is 1100. Order 2 means flip bit 2 (value 4): 1100 XOR 0100 = 1000 = 8. The merged block starts at 12 AND 8 = 8, and covers pfn 8 to 15. Note that 16 is wrong: 12 to 19 would not be aligned to 8.

blocks.question: `/proc/buddyinfo` shows thousands of free order-0 and order-1 blocks but zero free blocks at order 4 and above. A driver needs 64 KiB of physically contiguous memory (16 pages with 4 KiB pages). What is the most likely outcome?
options: It succeeds immediately, because enough pages are free in total
It fails or must wait for reclaim or compaction, because no free block of order 4 or higher exists
The buddy allocator merges non-adjacent order-1 blocks into one order-4 block
It succeeds, because buddy allocators have no external fragmentation
blocks.explain: 16 pages is order 4. Only buddies can merge, and only when both are free, so scattered small blocks cannot be combined. The kernel would have to reclaim or migrate pages (compaction) to create a large enough free block. When only virtual contiguity is needed, vmalloc avoids the problem by mapping scattered pages; a driver that needs physically contiguous memory cannot use it.

lessons.title: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects

blocks.md: Jeff Bonwick designed the **slab allocator** for the SunOS 5.4 kernel (USENIX 1994). His starting observation: for many kernel objects, *initializing and destroying* the object costs more than allocating its memory. An object with an embedded mutex, a condition variable and some list heads has to have them set up every time with `malloc`, and torn down every time with `free`.

The fix is **object caching**: keep freed objects in their *constructed* state, so the next allocation of that type can skip the setup. A client creates one cache per object type and gives it a constructor and destructor:

- `kmem_cache_create(name, size, align, constructor, destructor)` creates the cache.
- `kmem_cache_alloc(cache, flags)` returns an object that is already constructed.
- `kmem_cache_free(cache, obj)` returns it, still constructed.

The constructor runs only when memory first enters the cache; the destructor only when memory leaves it.

blocks.title: Bonwick: frequent kernel allocations with and without object caching

scenes.caption: Without caching (SPARCstation-2 timings in microseconds, from the 1994 paper). Each operation pays for constructing the object every time.

With caching. Speedups range from 1.4x (allocb) to 5.1x (shalloc): the more setup an object needs, the more caching saves. (The paper's table also lists makepipe, 126 to 98 us, left out here for scale.)

blocks.md:
Under each cache sits the data structure that gave the allocator its name. A **slab** is one or more pages carved into equal-size objects, plus a **reference count** of how many are allocated and a free list of the rest.

For small objects (under 1/8 of a page) Bonwick stores the slab's bookkeeping at the end of the page itself, and each free object holds the free-list link inside its own memory. So finding the slab of an object is pure address arithmetic, and one TLB entry covers the objects and their metadata.

Take a cache of 400-byte objects on 4096-byte pages, ignoring the small metadata as Bonwick's example does. One slab holds $\lfloor 4096 / 400 \rfloor = 10$ objects and leaves 96 bytes over, that is 9.6 bytes per object, or 2.4 percent waste. In general, if a slab holds $n$ objects the waste is at most $1/n$, so the allocator controls internal fragmentation by choosing the slab size; SunOS capped it at 1/8.

blocks.title: One slab of 400-byte objects: allocate, free, reuse

scenes.caption: The cache grows: it takes a page from the page allocator, cuts it into 10 objects and runs the constructor on each. 96 bytes at the end are left over. refcount = 0.
Three kmem_cache_alloc calls pop objects 0, 1, 2 off the slab's free list. No constructor runs: they were built when the slab was created. refcount = 3.
Object 1 is freed. It goes back on the free list still constructed (its lock is still initialized). refcount = 2. Simplified: here the freed object becomes the head of the list.
The next allocation gets object 1 back immediately, with no construction cost. This is the whole point of object caching. refcount = 3.
After seven more allocations all 10 objects are in use (refcount = 10). The next allocation must use another slab, or grow the cache with a new page.

blocks.md: A cache usually owns many slabs, kept in three groups: slabs with every object allocated, slabs with some free, and slabs with every object free. (Linux calls these *full*, *partial* and *free*; Bonwick's paper confusingly calls a fully allocated slab "empty" and a fully free one "complete".) Allocation prefers partial slabs, so completely free slabs accumulate where they can be handed back. Reclaiming is trivial: when a slab's refcount reaches zero, its pages can return to the page supplier. No neighbor search or coalescing is needed.

blocks.title: Slabs moving between lists as a cache grows and shrinks

scenes.caption: An empty cache: no slabs yet. The back end (grow, reap) is the only link to real memory.
First allocation: the cache grows by one slab from the page allocator. S1 now has 1 of 10 objects in use, so it sits on the partial list.
Nine more allocations fill S1. With nothing free it moves to the all-allocated list, where the allocator ignores it until something is freed.
The 11th allocation finds no partial slab, so the cache grows again: S2 joins the partial list.
All 10 objects in S1 are freed. Its refcount hits 0 and it moves to the all-free list. It is not returned at once: the next burst may need it (Bonwick kept a 15-second working set).
Memory pressure: the VM asks caches to give memory back, and S1's page goes back to the page allocator in one step. Only a refcount was needed, no coalescing.

blocks.md:
Two more reasons slabs fragment less. First, a cache only ever holds one size, so it can never pile up useless slivers left over from splitting bigger blocks. Second, objects of one type tend to have similar lifetimes, so a slab is less likely to be pinned by a single long-lived object.

Bonwick also noticed a hardware effect. Power-of-two allocators place every object at the start of a 512-byte (or 256, 1024) boundary. If the hot fields are the first 48 bytes of a 512-byte buffer, all objects hit the same cache sets and only 48/512, about 9 percent, of the cache is useful. **Slab coloring** shifts each new slab's first object by a different small offset, using the slab's leftover bytes. For 200-byte objects with 8-byte alignment, 20 objects use 4000 bytes, metadata 32, leaving 64: the colors are 0, 8, 16, ..., 64, then repeat.

blocks.prompt: Bonwick's alloc + free benchmark (no construction costs) measured 3.8 us for `kmem_cache_alloc`, 4.7 us for slab-backed `kmem_alloc`, 4.1 us for the 4.4BSD power-of-two allocator, and 9.4 us for the SVr4 buddy allocator. Why might `kmem_cache_alloc` beat `kmem_alloc` from the same allocator?
blocks.reveal: Because `kmem_cache_alloc` is handed the cache directly, while `kmem_alloc(size)` first has to work out which of its roughly 30 generic size caches (8 bytes to 9 KiB) to use. The paper also notes a mutex enter and exit pair cost 1.0 us, so locking alone set a 2.0 us floor for alloc plus free; the segregated-storage designs were close to it.

blocks.md: Slab = one cache per object size or type, slabs of whole pages cut into equal objects, a refcount per slab for trivial reclaim, and objects kept constructed between uses. It removes most of both internal and external fragmentation for small, frequent objects.

blocks.question: A slab holds 31 objects of 128 bytes in a 4096-byte page, with 32 bytes of in-page metadata. Without coloring, every slab's objects start at offset 0. What does coloring change?
options: It fits a 32nd object into the page by moving the metadata elsewhere
It uses the 96 leftover bytes to start each new slab's objects at a different offset, so hot fields of objects in different slabs map to different cache sets
It rounds the objects up to 256 bytes so each one is cache-line aligned
It marks freed objects with a pattern so use-after-free is detected
blocks.explain: 31 x 128 = 3968 bytes, plus 32 metadata leaves 96 spare bytes. Coloring spends that otherwise wasted space on an offset that varies per slab. (Filling freed memory with 0xdeadbeef is a separate debugging feature.)

blocks.question: Why can the slab allocator reclaim memory without the coalescing step a buddy allocator needs?
options: Because it never returns memory to the system
Because objects are always freed in the order they were allocated
Because a slab is a whole page-sized unit with a refcount: when the count reaches zero the entire slab goes back, no matter where its neighbors are
Because slab objects are always 2^k bytes and aligned like buddies
blocks.explain: The slab, not the object, is the unit exchanged with the page allocator. Freeing an object only decrements its slab's count; when it hits zero the slab's pages return in one step.

lessons.title: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose

blocks.md: The three designs are rarely used alone. The Linux kernel is the clearest example. At the bottom, the **buddy page allocator** manages physical memory in blocks of $2^k$ pages. On top of it, the **slab layer** asks for whole slabs of pages and carves them into objects. Kernel code calls `kmem_cache_create` for frequently used types (the kernel's proc documentation cites network buffers and the directory cache), and calls `kmalloc(size)` for everything else, which is served from a set of generic caches, one per size class.

blocks.title: Where a kernel allocation actually comes from

scenes.caption: kmalloc(100) picks the smallest generic cache that fits. On a typical x86-64 build the classes are 8, 16, 32, 64, 96, 128, 192, 256, then powers of two, so 100 bytes come from kmalloc-128.
Usually a partial slab has a free object and the call ends here. Only when the cache has none does it request pages from the buddy allocator to build a new slab.
Hot types get their own cache via kmem_cache_create, so objects are exactly the right size and can be grouped by type.
Large buffers that need not be physically contiguous use vmalloc, which maps pages that need not be physically contiguous into one virtual range, avoiding high-order buddy requests.

blocks.md:
The size-class rounding in `kmalloc` is internal fragmentation, measured in the same way as for buddy blocks. Using the class list from the kernel's `__kmalloc_index` (with an 8-byte minimum, as on x86-64):

- `kmalloc(100)` gets 128 bytes: 28 wasted (21.9 percent).
- `kmalloc(129)` gets 192: 63 wasted (32.8 percent).
- `kmalloc(300)` gets 512: 212 wasted (41.4 percent), because there is no class between 256 and 512.

The 96 and 192 classes exist precisely to soften the worst power-of-two cases. A type you allocate millions of times deserves its own cache.

A note on names. The kernel's slab layer has had several implementations. The original **SLAB** followed Bonwick's design with per-CPU and per-node queues. **SLUB** (Christoph Lameter, 2007) dropped most of those queues and moved per-slab metadata out of the slab and into the kernel's per-page metadata, keeping only a free list threaded through the free objects. SLOB was removed in Linux 6.4 and SLAB in 6.8, so SLUB is now the kernel's only slab allocator, even though the interface is still called "slab". To inspect caches, read `/proc/slabinfo`.

blocks.title: Bonwick 1994: total fragmentation under one workload sequence

scenes.caption: After boot on a 16 MB SPARCstation-1, each allocator ported into the same SunOS 5.4 kernel. Sequential fit starts best here.
After a spike: 256 processes each open a socket, then exit. The power-of-two and buddy designs jump past 40 percent waste.
After a find over /usr: almost unchanged.
After the kenbus timesharing benchmark (results are cumulative). Slab ends at 14 percent, about half of the next best. Measured in one 1994 setup; your workload will differ.

blocks.md:
**Choosing a design** comes down to what your objects look like:

- **Many objects with one shared lifetime** (per request, per frame, per compiler pass): an arena. Fastest possible allocation, free is a reset, but no individual frees and no destructors unless you add them.
- **Many objects of one type or size, freed individually**: a slab-style cache or pool. Constant-time alloc and free, low waste, objects can stay initialized.
- **Power-of-two chunks that must be contiguous and merge back** (pages, DMA buffers, a GPU or shared-memory pool): a buddy allocator.
- **Anything else**: a general-purpose malloc. Modern ones such as jemalloc and tcmalloc are mostly size classes (slab-like) on top of page-level management.

A pool or arena that never returns memory looks like a leak from the outside. Bonwick's caches give memory back under VM pressure; your custom pool should have some way to shrink (reset, trim, or a size cap).

Next in this track: memory fragmentation in depth, then thread caches and magazines (how per-CPU front ends remove the lock from slab allocation), then how jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc combine all of these.

blocks.question: A game allocates thousands of temporary objects while building each frame, and none of them is needed after the frame is drawn. Which allocator fits best?
options: A buddy allocator, so the temporary objects can merge back into big blocks
A slab cache per object type, so each object can be freed individually
The general-purpose malloc, because the objects have different sizes
A per-frame bump arena that is reset after the frame is drawn
blocks.explain: All objects share one lifetime that ends at a known point, which is exactly the phase-oriented pattern bump allocation is built for: each allocation is a pointer add and freeing the whole frame is one reset.

blocks.question: A driver calls `kmalloc(260)` a million times. Roughly how much memory is lost to size-class rounding, and what is the usual fix?
options: About 0.25 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 512; give the type its own kmem_cache
Nothing, because kmalloc returns exactly the requested size
About 0.06 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 320; use vmalloc instead
About 0.5 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 1024; allocate whole pages with alloc_pages
blocks.explain: The classes go 256 then 512, so each 260-byte request occupies 512 bytes: 252 bytes x 1,000,000 = 252 MB, about 0.25 GB. A dedicated cache sized for the object (kmem_cache_create) removes almost all of that waste.

blocks.question: In the kernel stack above, which layer is responsible for merging freed memory back into larger contiguous blocks?
options: The kmalloc size classes
The buddy page allocator
Each slab's free list
vmalloc
blocks.explain: Slabs reclaim by refcount and hand whole pages back; the buddy allocator then merges those pages with their buddies into higher-order blocks.
